example_01.category: Unnecessary role binding to authenticated users for a non-authenticated workload
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods in the webapp namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage pods in the webapp namespace without needing to authenticate first. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not show the need for such broad access.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users for monitoring purposes
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all resources in the cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can access all cluster resources for monitoring purposes. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, while the binding file alone does not restrict access to just the monitored resources.

example_03.category: Unnecessary service account access for unauthenticated users in the CI/CD namespace
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants create, list, update, and patch permissions on deployments. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can perform these actions in the cicd namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being bound to system:unauthenticated.

example_04.category: Unnecessary secret access for database operations
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can read all secrets in the database namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_05.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on nodes and persistent volumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate node information in the infrastructure namespace as well as access persistent volumes. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subjects, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_06.category: Unnecessary role binding to authenticated users for non-authenticated access
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants write permissions on configmaps and pods in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can now perform these actions without needing a password or token. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, while the binding file alone does not restrict access to non-authenticated users.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants create, list, get, update, and patch permissions on serviceaccounts. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can create new service accounts across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, while the binding file alone does not restrict access to just the intended users.

example_08.category: Unnecessary pod exec access for unauthenticated users in the development namespace
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can perform pod exec operations in the development namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_09.category: Insecure network policy for unauthenticated users
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on ingress resources. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all ingress resources in the ingress-nginx namespace. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to unauthenticated users.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users for multi-tenant self-service
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants full administrative access within tenant namespaces, including pods, services, configmaps, secrets, serviceaccounts, and persistentvolumeclaims. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, allowing any authenticated user to have full namespace admin rights for multi-tenant self-service. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the dangerous subjects it applies to.

example_11.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running Nginx:1.25 and explicitly states it serves static HTTP content with no backend API calls or credential access required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods, deployments, and services in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload has no legitimate need for service account access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_12.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Redis cache workload running the image redis:7.2 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to configmaps for configuration purposes. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and deployments. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the service account redis-cache-sa within the caching namespace only. Reading all four files together confirms the service account has been granted unnecessary access — it needs no pod or deployment-specific permissions since the workload is running in a configmap for configuration purposes.

example_13.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_13.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus metrics scraper workload running prom/prometheus:v2.47.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it collects pod and service metrics for monitoring purposes. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, and delete permissions on pods and services within the monitoring namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload legitimately needs access to pod and service metrics for monitoring but has been granted permissions on sensitive resources that could be exploited if improperly used.

example_14.category: Unnecessary network policy for a service that does not require it
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static file server workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves uploaded assets over HTTP, without requiring any network access beyond the service account's permissions. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on services via resourceGroups scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that a network policy is unnecessary for this workload — it only needs access to its own service account and does not require any external network resources.

example_15.category: Unnecessary role and binding granting access to all pods in the database namespace
example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database workload running Postgres:15. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on all pods in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together — the workload needs access to PostgreSQL for its operations and the role/binding grant it unrestricted access to all pods in the database namespace. No cross-resource permission relationships create necessary or appropriate risk.

example_16.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a React frontend application workload running node:20-alpine and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves the user interface. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on services and endpoints within the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload needs access to sensitive resources (services and endpoints) but has been granted exactly that via the service account.

example_17.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_17.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a nginx reverse proxy workload running Nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to the services and pods for routing traffic. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on all pods and resources within the proxy namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the nginx-proxy-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload needs access to services and pods for routing traffic, while the role grants exactly that access across multiple resources.

example_18.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_18.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch workload running elasticsearch:8.10.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, statefulsets, pods, and their resources for log storage operations. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on all these resources via the empty namespace scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the workload needs access to sensitive resources and the service account has been granted exactly that — a misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading across multiple manifest files.

example_19.category: Unnecessary RBAC permissions on non-privileged resources
example_19.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ message queue workload running the image rabbitmq:3.12-management and explicitly states it requires access to no secrets or services other than those provided by its own pod. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and services in the messaging namespace, including creating new ones via 'create' verbs. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment, which is not a privileged resource but rather an unprivileged pod that needs no such access. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the workload has legitimate need for none of these permissions, and the roles grant exactly those permissions.

example_20.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_20.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static nginx metrics exporter workload running the image nginx/nginx-prometheus-exporter:0.11 and explicitly states it exposes basic HTTP metrics endpoint via the containerPort 9113. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, delete permissions on deployments and pods in the exports namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the ServiceAccount nginx-exporter-sa within the same namespace. Reading all four files together reveals that the workload needs access only to HTTP metrics endpoints exposed via 9113, but it has been granted full control over sensitive resources including pods and services. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading across multiple manifest files.

example_21.category: Insecure Network Policy for a Web Application
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the frontend application is running on pod with labels 'app: frontend'. The network policy.yaml restricts ingress traffic to pods labeled 'role: ingress-controller', which does not match any of the frontend pods. This results in an insecure Network Policy, as it allows traffic from a role (ingress controller) that should never be allowed into the frontend application's pod.

example_22.category: Insecure network policy for database pods
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the postgres pod should be isolated from unauthorised ingress traffic. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows all pods in the namespace to access the postgres pod via both ingress and egress rules. This creates a security weakness because it exposes the database service to potential attacks or unauthorized access.

example_23.category: Insecure network policy for a sensitive service
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the Prometheus service with specific resource requests and limits. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress traffic to pods labeled 'role: metrics-consumer'. This combination creates an insecure situation because any pod running a Prometheus scraper (which is likely part of the monitoring cluster) could be inadvertently restricted from accessing the Prometheus service, potentially exposing it to unauthorized access or misconfiguration.

example_24.category: Insecure network policy for production environment pods
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the payment-api is running in a production environment with specific labels. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to only those pods matching the podSelector, which includes all pods labeled 'app: payment-api' and 'env: production'. This policy allows any pod from the 'role: api-gateway' role to access the payment-api pods, potentially exposing them to unauthorized traffic in a production environment. The misconfiguration is not apparent when reading either file alone but becomes clear by examining both together.

example_25.category: Insecure network policy for Elasticsearch pods, allowing unauthenticated access to logging agents
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the Elasticsearch pod should be isolated from other pods in the logging namespace. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows any pod with a label of 'role: log-shipper' to access the Elasticsearch pod, which is not restricted by the isolation policy. This misconfiguration exposes Elasticsearch pods to potential unauthorized access via unauthenticated agents.

example_26.category: Insecure network policy for RabbitMQ pods
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the RabbitMQ pod should be isolated from other pods in the messaging namespace. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress and egress traffic to any pod labeled 'app: worker', which includes all pods running message-broker-related workloads. This policy is not scoped correctly — it grants unrestricted access to all pods with a specific label, potentially exposing RabbitMQ pods to unauthorized communication.

example_27.category: Insecure network policy for Jenkins CI/CD controller pods
example_27.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins CI/CD controller named jenkins with specific resource requests and limits. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress traffic to only authorized build agents, but it does not specify any restrictions on the pods that can receive this policy. This results in an insecure network policy for all pods in the namespace, including those managed by the jenkins deployment. The misconfiguration is only apparent when reading both files together: the deployment establishes a specific set of pods needing ingress access, while the networkpolicy.yaml grants unrestricted ingress to any pod.

example_28.category: Insecure network policy for a sensitive application
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the React single-page application (react-app) is running on port 3000 and uses an image of node:20-alpine. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to pods labeled with 'role: ingress-controller'. This policy allows traffic from any pod in the frontend namespace, including those not part of the ingress controller's responsibility, which could potentially expose the React application to unauthorized access.

example_29.category: Insecure network policy for a critical service
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the API gateway workload running Nginx:1.25 on port 80 and 443, while the networkpolicy.yaml restricts traffic to only pods labeled with 'role' matching 'load-balancer'. The combination of these two files creates an insecure policy that allows external access to the API gateway without any additional security measures in place. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading both files together: the deployment exposes the service on public ports, while the networkpolicy restricts it to a specific pod label.

example_30.category: Inappropriate Network Policy for a Worker Pod
example_30.justification: The deployment.yaml specifies that the worker pods are part of a job-processor namespace and should be isolated from other pods. However, the network policy in networkpolicy.yaml is configured to allow ingress traffic only from pods labeled 'app: job-scheduler' and egress traffic only to pods labeled 'app: postgres'. This configuration does not align with the intended isolation for worker pods, which are supposed to restrict access to a specific service (job scheduler) rather than allowing unrestricted access. The misconfiguration is evident when reading both files together.

example_31.category: Overly broad ClusterRole granting full cluster administrative access to the platform engineering team, which is not scoped correctly for a CI/CD pipeline tooling role.
example_31.justification: The target_clusterrole.yaml grants non-resource URL verbs and all resource verbs on everything. This ClusterRole is bound to the cluster via the ClusterRoleBinding, which means any user with this binding can perform full administrative actions across the entire cluster. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to just the CI/CD pipeline tooling.

example_32.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for Prometheus service account
example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and escalate permissions on roles within the rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount in the monitoring namespace, which is a common service account used by Prometheus for its own purposes. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being bound to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount.

example_33.category: Unnecessary impersonation role for non-impersonating users
example_33.justification: The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the impersonation role to a service account that is not intended to be used for impersonation. The user binding grants cluster-admin privileges to an administrator, but the impersonation role itself does not require any users to impersonate — it only allows the API gateway to impersonate other users in delegated authentication flows. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading all three files together: the impersonation role alone does not reveal the intended use case, and the user binding grants privileges that are unnecessary for the service account's purpose.

example_34.category: Unnecessary role binding for a broad deployment role, potentially exposing sensitive operations to unauthorized users
example_34.justification: The devops-deployer role in the target_role.yaml is defined with verbs that allow it to perform actions on multiple resources including deployments, replicasets, statefulsets, pods, services, and configmaps. This broad scope grants access to sensitive operations such as creating, updating, deleting, and listing resources without proper authorization checks. The devops-role-binder-binding in the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to a user named 'devops-automation-user', which is not restricted by any specific namespace or resource type. This binding exposes the broad deployment capabilities of the devops-deployer role to anyone with access to the automation user, potentially allowing unauthorized users to perform sensitive operations on behalf of the devops team without proper authorization checks.

example_35.category: Cluster role with overly broad permissions to all resources and URLs, potentially exposing sensitive information or unauthorized access
example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants ClusterRole permissions to all resources in the RBAC API group (including non-resource URL operations) and all verbs. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to a security team group, which is not restricted by any specific resource or verb. This results in an overly broad permission that could expose sensitive information or potentially allow unauthorized access across the entire cluster.

example_36.category: Service account impersonation role bound to a service account with full cluster administrative access, creating unnecessary privilege escalation risk
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate and get permissions on all service accounts. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the workflow-engine-sa ServiceAccount, which is a high-privilege service account used by the platform's provisioning system. This binding allows any user with access to the workflow-engine-sa to impersonate any other service account in the cluster, including those with full administrative privileges (cluster-admin). The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_37.category: Overly broad ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding granting full administrative access to the platform automation service account, which is not necessary for RBAC management tasks.
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants all RBAC-related permissions (get, list, bind, escalate) on roles and clusterroles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount, which is not necessary for managing RBAC bindings or escalating roles. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive access needed.

example_38.justification: The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the infra-group-impersonator role to a user named 'infra-automation-user', which is not part of any system groups. The target_clusterrolebinding.yaml then binds this role to the group 'system:masters' via a ClusterRoleBinding, effectively impersonating the entire system:masters group. This creates an unnecessary security risk since it allows anyone with access to the cluster to impersonate all users in the system:masters group, potentially granting them full cluster administrative privileges without proper authorization checks. The misconfiguration is only apparent by reading these files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous binding, and the binding file alone does not show the necessary permissions being granted.

example_39.category: Overly broad ClusterRole granting permissions to all workloads across the cluster
example_39.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on deployments and daemonsets in the entire cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-engineers group, which means any user or service account within the cluster can now perform these operations across all workloads without needing a specific role binding. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to just the intended group.

example_40.category: Overly broad ClusterRole granting full administrative access to tenant namespaces, including secret and workload management
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all resources across the entire Kubernetes API. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount named tenant-provisioner-sa in the tenants namespace, which is expected for a service account used by a provisioning system. However, the role grants full administrative access within any tenant's namespaces, including secret and workload management — permissions that are not necessary or appropriate for a typical Kubernetes cluster configuration. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous scope of the ClusterRole, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for a static web server
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a web application using Nginx and explicitly states it serves pre-built static HTML files with no backend or credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants read access to all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the service account used by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: while the workload needs access to its own secret for static content serving, the role binding grants it access to all secrets in the entire namespace, which is unnecessary and potentially dangerous.

example_42.category: Unnecessary secret access for a service that does not require credentials or secrets
example_42.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the Prometheus node exporter workload running prom/node-exporter:v1.6.0 and explicitly states it exposes host-level hardware and OS metrics only, requiring no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get access to all secrets in the monitoring namespace via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the node-exporter-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the secret access is unnecessary and improperly scoped — the workload legitimately does not need any credentials or secrets for its purpose.

example_43.category: Unnecessary secret access for a non-authenticated service
example_43.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the blackbox-exporter workload running Prometheus's blackbox exporter, which probes unauthenticated public HTTP and ICMP endpoints. The role.yaml grants read access to secrets in the probing namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the blackbox-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the workload needs no secret access for its purpose, and the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_44.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Memcached service and its annotation explicitly states it requires no Kubernetes secrets. The role.yaml grants read access to all secrets in the caching namespace via resource scoping, but this is only relevant because of how the rolebinding.yaml binds the role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all four files together confirms that there are no unnecessary permissions or cross-resource relationships that create a security weakness.

example_45.category: Unnecessary secret access for Prometheus Metrics Exporter
example_45.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a StatsD exporter workload running prom/statsd-exporter:v0.26.0 and explicitly states it requires no credentials or secrets for Prometheus metrics exposure. However, the role.yaml grants get access to all secrets in the metrics namespace via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the secret access is both necessary and appropriately scoped — the workload legitimately needs no credentials for Prometheus metrics exposure, but it has been granted exactly that.

example_46.category: Unnecessary secret access for a web server without TLS
example_46.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Caddy web server serving pre-built React static assets over HTTP on port 80 only, no TLS configuration, and no backend integration. The role.yaml grants read access to secrets in the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the caddy-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the web server has been granted unnecessary secret access for a static asset serving without TLS configuration or any backend integration. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading across multiple manifest files.

example_47.category: Unnecessary secret access for Prometheus Graphite exporter
example_47.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus Graphite exporter workload running prom/graphite-exporter:0.13.3 and explicitly states it requires access to secrets in the redis namespace for receiving Graphite metrics over TCP and exposing them as Prometheus metrics, no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the redis namespace via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-exporter-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the secret access is both necessary and appropriately scoped — the workload legitimately needs credentials for Graphite metrics but access is restricted to exactly those specific secrets.

example_48.category: Unnecessary secret access for a simple HTTP health check
example_48.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a curl-based HTTP healthcheck probe that polls public service endpoints only, requiring no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get access to all secrets in the staging namespace via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the healthcheck-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms the secret access is both unnecessary and improperly scoped — a simple HTTP health check legitimately needs no credentials, and the binding restricts it to exactly that one secret.

example_49.category: Unnecessary secret access for a static web server
example_49.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Apache httpd server serving static documentation content over HTTP only, no dynamic backend, and no TLS configuration. The role.yaml grants read access to secrets in the docs namespace for the Apache httpd workload. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the service account httpd-sa mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration is only apparent when reading all four files together: the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding grant it exactly that.

example_50.category: Unnecessary secret access for a Traefik service
example_50.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the whoami diagnostic service that returns HTTP request metadata only, no credentials or secrets required. The role.yaml grants read access to all secrets in the whoami namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the whoami-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. This misconfiguration allows any user with a secret reader role (which could be anyone) to access sensitive information from Traefik's configuration and logs without proper authorization. By reading all four files together, it becomes clear that the service does not need read access to secrets.

example_76.category: Unnecessary role binding to authenticated users for unauthenticated operations
example_76.justification: The role.yaml grants management access on PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) in the storage namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage PVCs in the storage namespace without needing a valid service account or cluster admin credentials. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not show the need for such access.

example_77.category: Unnecessary secret access for unauthenticated users across the entire cluster
example_77.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all secrets across the entire cluster namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_78.category: Unnecessary NetworkPolicy management for authenticated users in the API namespace
example_78.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all NetworkPolicies in the api namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all NetworkPolicies in the API namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being managed.

example_79.category: Overly broad ClusterRole binding to authenticated users
example_79.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'platform-role-binder' with permissions to bind other roles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the system:authenticated group, allowing any authenticated user access to bind ClusterRoles. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_80.category: ServiceAccount token creation misconfiguration for unauthenticated users
example_80.justification: The role.yaml grants create permissions on the serviceaccounts/token resource in the staging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create ServiceAccount tokens in the staging namespace without needing a token themselves. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the sensitive permission being granted, and the binding file alone does not restrict access to unauthenticated users.

example_81.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_81.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Grafana dashboard workload running the image grafana/grafana:10.0.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to configmaps and services for visualizing metrics. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on all resources within the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the grafana-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that Grafana needs access to sensitive resources like configmaps and services for its dashboard operations, but it has been granted exactly those permissions via the service account alone. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all manifest files together.

example_82.category: Unnecessary service account access to sensitive resources
example_82.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins CI server workload running jenkins/jenkins:2.414.3-lts and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to sensitive resources such as pods, service accounts, and deployments. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on all these resources. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the jenkins-sa ServiceAccount which is mounted by the deployment. example_74.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an API gateway workload running nginx:1.25.3 and explicitly states it requires access to its TLS certificate secret for HTTPS termination, mounted as a volume. However, the role.yaml grants get access to only the api-gateway-tls secret via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the TLS certificate access is both necessary and improperly scoped — the workload legitimately needs access for HTTPS termination, but it has been granted read-only access to a secret that is not needed for any other purpose.

example_75.category: Unnecessary secret access for a workload that does not require it
example_75.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the queue-worker service running Python:3.11.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires access to RabbitMQ credentials for message queue authentication. However, the role.yaml grants get access to only the rabbitmq-credentials secret via resourceNames scoping. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the queue-worker-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms that the workload does not need RabbitMQ credentials for message queue authentication, and the misconfiguration is only visible when these files are read together.

example_116.category: Unnecessary service account access for cluster-level permissions
example_116.justification: The rolebinding.yaml binds the monitoring-pod-reader ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount named monitoring-sa within the monitoring namespace. This means that any user or group bound to this ServiceAccount can access all pods in the monitoring namespace, which is an unnecessary and potentially dangerous level of access for a cluster-level permission. The misconfiguration only becomes apparent by reading both files together: the rolefile grants read-only access on pods, while the binding file restricts it to the monitoring namespace.

example_117.category: Unnecessary role binding to a group with no specific resources or permissions defined for that group
example_117.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named logging-configmap-reader, which grants read access to configmaps. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the Group 'logging-team' within the namespace 'logging'. This binding is unnecessary because there are no specific resources or permissions defined for the 'logging-team' group in any of the files provided. It only creates a security weakness when combined with other files that define sensitive resources and permissions.

example_118.category: Unnecessary role binding to a user with cluster scope permissions
example_118.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read-only access to deployments for the CI/CD pipeline operator. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to a User named cicd-pipeline-operator within the cicd namespace, which has no specific need or legitimate reason for accessing any deployment resources. This misconfiguration is only apparent by reading both files together: the clusterrole establishes the scope of access, while the rolebinding grants it to an unprivileged user with no defined purpose.

example_119.category: Unnecessary secret access for sensitive data
example_119.justification: The role.yaml grants read access to the database-credentials secret within the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the database-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by a pod that uses the database service account for its secrets. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the workload legitimately needs access to sensitive data (the database credentials), and the binding grants exactly that access.

example_120.category: Unnecessary job access for non-privileged users
example_120.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read-only access to jobs in the ml namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the ml-team Group, which is not a service account or user group typically associated with job management within Kubernetes. This misconfiguration allows any non-privileged user (e.g., from outside the ml team) to view all jobs in the ml namespace without proper authorization, potentially exposing sensitive information or allowing unauthorized access.
